page.title: Capacity and memory
page.description: Size a tinyactors host, read what it uses, and see what an actor costs and how each operation's cost holds as the population doubles.

hero.headline: Size a host for its population.
hero.lede: A started actor takes about 530 bytes on Node.js and a hibernated one about 120. Each operation costs about the same at four million actors as at two.

section.heading: A host grows one region per image.
section.p: A host keeps its actors in blocks of memory, one region per segment, that is per image. It sizes each from its config, and grows one when something in it runs out.
Leave the sizes to the host, or size a host up front for the population you expect.

section.heading: Sizes are where pools start, not limits.
section.p: The config option's system map gives each new segment its first sizes. Each key is a whole number, and an absent key or 0 is the default.

row.cell: events waiting in the actors' queues
actors in the middle of a step at once (a sender keeps its workspace until its send is handled); never refused: an actor waits for one, and the host adds more
derived from the image and maxActors

section.p: When a pool fills, the host grows that segment between runs. The new region has more of what ran out, and the rest as it was.
A pool doubles, or grows up to 16 times at once if doubling adds under a quarter of the region. So a small pool beside a large region grows in a few copies, in proportion to itself.
A grown region never shrinks, and maxActors is at most 8,388,606.
A run or an input is refused with TA_ERROR_NO_MEMORY only at a pool's largest size, or when the allocator refuses memory.

section.heading: hostStats reports each pool's use and high water.
section.p: host.hostStats () answers with pools, one entry per live segment, in segment order. An entry's segment is its place among new Host's charts, or what addImage returned.
For actors, events, timers, workspaces, requests and slabBytes, an entry gives the pool's capacity, its used and its highWater. slabBytes is the instance and string memory.
Each segment grows on its own, so two images, or a migration's old and new versions, are two entries.

example.code: maxActors default: capacity 64, then 1000 used, high water 1000, grown: true segments reported: 0, 1 maxActors 1000: capacity 1000, then 1000 used, high water 1000, grown: false segments reported: 0, 1

section.p: To size a host up front, run a realistic load, read the high-water marks, and give the next host those sizes. host.hostConfig() answers the sizes a host was made with, every default filled in.

section.heading: Size a known population up front.
section.p: Each growth copies the region, and a grown region keeps its size. A host that will hold a known population is better sized for it.
A hibernated actor keeps its slot and its record, about 64 bytes, so maxActors counts every actor. The instance and string memory are for the resident ones only.
The repository's hibernation gate sizes a host for R resident actors out of N, for a counter of a few variables:
A chart with more variables or longer strings needs more per resident actor. Read slabBytes.highWater under load to see how much.

section.heading: An actor takes about 530 bytes.
section.p: The memory program measures the resident memory one more actor, message and delayed send adds to a process, the host included. Run it with your runtime, datamodel, chart and data:

table.caption: A million actors. Measured 2026-11-20 on an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5 and Bun 1.4.1. A counter chart with one <data>, messages of {"text": "hello"}, tracing on; the hibernated column keeps at most 1000 actors resident and the rest in a store.

section.p: A host's and an engine's fixed costs spread over the population, so an actor costs less in a larger one.

table.caption: Node.js on the native datamodel, the same run.

section.p: The run's CSV holds each row at every population and on every runtime, to compare with a chart of your own.

section.p: What a chart's scripts declare adds nothing per actor. Its helpers are the chart's, made once, and a top-level var is one more variable (Writing charts).

section.heading: Twice the actors, the same cost.
section.p: tools/scale.mjs times every operation of the API on N actors and on 2N, each host in its own process.
It fails when an operation costs more than 1.5 times as much at 2N. The cost is per call on one actor, and per actor on the whole population.
Most of the actors are hibernated in SQLite, and one in a hundred runs an invoked service. Then the same runs with every actor resident.
Each cell is the cost at N, then at 2N, in microseconds, and their ratio. Every operation passed.

table.section: Work does not grow with the population
table.caption: Hibernated: 2,000,000 and 4,000,000 actors, at most 1000 counters resident, 20,000 and 40,000 actors each running an invoked service. One run, alone on the machine, 2026-11-20: an Intel Xeon at 2.10 GHz, 4 CPUs, 16 GiB, Linux; Node.js 22.23.5 and Bun 1.4.1.

table.section: Work does not grow with the population
table.caption: All resident: 1,000,000 and 2,000,000 actors, the same run.

section.p: Two million resident actors take up to 5.2 GiB on quickjs. So four million do not fit in 16 GiB beside the scenario's other work.

table.caption: Peak resident memory at N and 2N, in MiB, the same run.

section.p: The run's files, every operation and sample, are in tools/results/2026-11-20. mise run scale in tinyactors-napi writes them to build/scale-*.json.
The repository's published numbers rules say when to run it again.
